thread_tweets.text:
3️⃣ Open interest vs volume
Volume tells us how much was traded over a period, while open interest (OI) tells us the value of positions still open at a given moment.

A trader can open and close positions all day, adding to volume each time, but finish with no open position.

So @HyperliquidX’s lead here means it holds the largest share of open positions by value, but it doesn’t mean it has the most traders or that every market is easy to exit.

tweets.full_text:
These charts from @castle_labs caught my eye, so here's what I think they mean for traders ↓

1️⃣ More perp trading is moving onchain

this chart shows perp DEXs taking a bigger share of global perp trading volume, from 0.11% to 12.33%.

That means a bigger share of perp trading is happening onchain, but it doesn’t tell us whether more people are trading or the same traders are simply trading more.

I’d want to see how much of that activity sticks around after rewards end.

2️⃣ Onchain trading is expanding beyond crypto

What stands out to me is that RWA volume grew alongside its share of onchain trading through July, which suggests trading activity was broadening beyond crypto.

But this is trading volume, so it doesn’t mean that much money was invested in the underlying assets.

3️⃣ Open interest vs volume
Volume tells us how much was traded over a period, while open interest (OI) tells us the value of positions still open at a given moment.

A trader can open and close positions all day, adding to volume each time, but finish with no open position.

So @HyperliquidX’s lead here means it holds the largest share of open positions by value, but it doesn’t mean it has the most traders or that every market is easy to exit.

My takeaway: more perp trading is moving onchain, and the range of assets is growing, but I’d still look beyond headline volume to understand what’s driving that activity and whether it lasts.

Which perp venue are you using most right now, and what keeps you there?

tweets.text:
My two cents in the @Starknet proposal is that companies and ecosystems should always pursue product market fit beyond all else. 

If becoming an L1 helps them with PMF, then they should race ahead and go for it. 

Staying, or becoming an L2, shouldn’t rely upon cult alignment. It should simply be the best business decision from features, operational costs, access to liquidity etc. 

Answering those questions will depend on the teams business objectives and technical capabilities. 

Many teams will benefit from becoming L2s, others who are willing to have higher operational costs and are technically capable, may simply want to go the L1 route. 

I hope they do what is best for themselves and their users.
